section.title: The Birth of Samuel
section.sectionRationale: The book opens not in a palace but in the ache of a barren woman. Elkanah has two wives; Peninnah has children and taunts, Hannah has none and weeps. At Shiloh, where a corrupt priesthood is failing, Hannah pours out her soul to the LORD of Hosts and vows that a son given to her will be given back to Him. God remembers her, Samuel is born, and Hannah brings him to the house of the LORD. It is one movement: the LORD raises up a deliverer through the prayer of a lowly, forgotten woman.
section.thesis: When the leadership of Israel is bankrupt and one woman is empty and despised, the LORD who closes and opens the womb hears a prayer poured out in anguish, gives the son who is asked, and receives him back, quietly beginning the rescue of His people through the lowly rather than the powerful.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the barren wife and her rival, verses 1 to 8; the vow poured out at Shiloh, verses 9 to 18; the LORD remembers and Samuel is born, verses 19 to 20; and the child given back to the LORD, verses 21 to 28.

units.label: The barren wife and her rival
units.note: the LORD had closed her womb

verses.text: Now there was a man named Elkanah who was from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim. He was the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives, one named Hannah and the other Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
Year after year Elkanah would go up from his city to worship and sacrifice to the {{tsebaoth|LORD of Hosts}} at Shiloh, where Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests to the LORD.
And whenever the day came for Elkanah to present his sacrifice, he would give portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But to Hannah he would give a double portion, for he loved her even though the LORD had closed her womb.
Because the LORD had closed Hannah’s womb, her rival would provoke her viciously to taunt her.
And this went on year after year. Whenever Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, her rival taunted her until she wept and would not eat.
“Hannah, why are you crying?” her husband Elkanah asked. “Why won’t you eat? Why is your heart so grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”

units.label: The vow poured out at Shiloh
units.note: I have poured out my soul before the LORD

verses.text: So after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh, Hannah stood up. Now Eli the priest was sitting on a chair by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.
In her bitter distress, Hannah prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears.

And she made a vow, saying, “O LORD of Hosts, if only You will look upon the affliction of Your maidservant and remember me, not forgetting Your maidservant but giving her a son, then I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no {{nazir|razor}} shall ever touch his head.”
As Hannah kept on praying before the LORD, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was praying in her heart, and though her lips were moving, her voice could not be heard. So Eli thought she was drunk
and said to her, “How long will you be drunk? Put away your wine!”
“No, my lord,” Hannah replied. “I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have not had any wine or strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
Do not take your servant for a wicked woman, for all this time I have been praying out of the depth of my anguish and grief.”
“Go in peace,” Eli replied, “and may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him.”
“May your maidservant find favor with you,” said Hannah. Then she went on her way, and she began to eat, and her face was no longer downcast.

units.label: The LORD remembers and Samuel is born

verses.text: The next morning they got up early to bow in worship before the LORD, and then they returned home to Ramah. And Elkanah had relations with his wife Hannah, and the LORD {{zakar|remembered}} her.
So in the course of time, Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, saying, “Because I have {{shaal|asked}} for him from the LORD.”

units.label: The child given back to the LORD
units.note: he is dedicated to the LORD

verses.text: Then Elkanah and all his house went up to make the annual sacrifice to the LORD and to fulfill his vow,
but Hannah did not go. “After the boy is weaned,” she said to her husband, “I will take him to appear before the LORD and to stay there permanently.”
“Do what you think is best,” her husband Elkanah replied, “and stay here until you have weaned him. Only may the LORD confirm His word.” So Hannah stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him.

Once she had weaned him, Hannah took the boy with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine. Though the boy was still young, she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh.
And when they had slaughtered the bull, they brought the boy to Eli.
“Please, my lord,” said Hannah, “as surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD.
I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him,
I now dedicate the boy to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD.” So they worshiped the LORD there.

tsebaoth.gloss: Hosts, armies. The title LORD of Hosts, first used in Scripture here at Shiloh, names the LORD as commander of the armies of heaven and earth. It is fitting that the book which raises up kings and fights the LORD's battles opens by naming Him the true King over every host.

nazir.gloss: One separated or consecrated, a Nazirite. Hannah's vow that no razor will touch her son's head sets him apart to the LORD for life, like Samson before him, Numbers 6. Samuel is given wholly to God from the womb, a life marked out as belonging entirely to the LORD.

zakar.gloss: To remember, call to mind, act on behalf of. When Scripture says the LORD remembered Hannah, it does not mean He had forgotten; it means He moved to act on His covenant care, as He remembered Noah and Israel in Egypt. God's remembering is always the prelude to His saving deed.

shaal.gloss: To ask, request, or lend. It threads through the whole chapter: Hannah asked for a son, the LORD granted what she asked, and she gives him back as one asked of, and lent to, the LORD. The same root stands behind the name Saul, the king Israel will later ask for; here it names a son asked in faith and returned in worship.

basic.context: The book of 1 Samuel opens in a dark time. The judges have failed, the priesthood at Shiloh is corrupt, and there is no king. Into that emptiness comes a barren, grieving woman named Hannah, tormented by her husband's other wife. Year after year she goes up to worship and comes home in tears. Then at Shiloh she pours out her soul to the LORD of Hosts and vows that if He gives her a son, she will give him back to God for life. God remembers her, Samuel is born, and Hannah keeps her word and brings the little boy to live in God's house. The question underneath it all is: where will Israel's rescue come from? The answer, surprisingly, is through the prayer of a lowly, forgotten woman.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, telling us what actually happened, not simply giving us a model to copy. Hannah is not rewarded because she bargained well; the point is that God delights to lift up the lowly and to work His salvation through the weak and overlooked. We should not turn her vow into a formula for getting what we want from God. The abiding truths are that God hears the brokenhearted, that He opens and closes the womb, and that He is quietly beginning to raise up a deliverer when Israel is at its lowest.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens by naming the LORD of Hosts, tsebaoth, the commander of heaven's armies, the true King over Israel. Hannah vows her son as a nazir, one set apart to God, no razor touching his head. The turning point is that the LORD zakar, remembered, Hannah, His remembering always moving Him to act. And the whole story turns on the word shaal, to ask: Hannah asked for a son, God granted her request, and she gives him back as one asked of and lent to the LORD.
basic.typology: Hannah's song of a womb opened by God foreshadows another miraculous birth announced to a lowly woman, Mary, whose song echoes Hannah's own. Samuel, given wholly to God from the womb to serve in the house of the LORD, points ahead to the true Prophet and Priest who does always the will of His Father. And a barren woman given a son by God's power is a recurring sign that salvation is His gift, not human achievement.
basic.christ: The God who opens the barren womb and raises up a deliverer from an obscure hill town is the same God who, in the fullness of time, would send His Son through a lowly virgin in an obscure town called Bethlehem. Hannah's prayer, and the song that follows it in chapter 2, sets the key for the whole story of salvation: God brings down the proud and lifts up the humble. Samuel, the asked-for son given back to God, dimly points to the Son whom the Father gives and who gives Himself back in perfect obedience.
basic.god: This chapter shows a God who is not distant from the tears of the overlooked. He is the LORD of Hosts, sovereign over armies, yet He bends to hear one weeping woman. He is the God who opens and closes the womb, who remembers, and who gives. And He is beginning, quietly and gently, to answer the chaos of the age of the judges, not with a mighty man but with a praying woman and a little boy.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 30 and other barren-mother stories show God giving life where there was none. Luke 1 records Mary's song, which deliberately echoes Hannah's. Psalm 113 sings of the God who lifts the needy and gives the barren woman a home. And 1 Peter 5 promises that God gives grace to the humble.
basic.oneStory: At the lowest point of the judges, God begins Israel's rescue through the prayer of a barren woman. The son He gives, Samuel, will anoint the kings through whom the promise runs, and the pattern set here, God lifting the lowly and giving the asked-for son, runs straight through the story to Bethlehem, where God gives His own Son to save His people.

context.literary:
The chapter is framed by two nearly identical journeys to Shiloh that end in opposite moods. The opening pilgrimage, repeated year after year, verses 3 and 7, produces only provoking and weeping, a ritual that has become an occasion for pain rather than joy; the closing pilgrimage, undertaken once Samuel is weaned, produces worship, gift giving, and a settled dedication, so that the narrator lets the reader feel, through simple repetition of form, how completely Hannah's situation has turned.

Dialogue dominates the unit far more than narration; nearly every verse from 8 to 28 is direct speech, Elkanah's clumsy comfort, Hannah's vow, Eli's misjudgment and correction, the final exchange at the sanctuary, so that the chapter reads almost like a small drama in four scenes rather than a report of events. This density of speech puts weight on what people say about grief, prayer, and God rather than on the bare facts of what happened, fitting a chapter whose real subject is the inner life of a woman no one but the LORD is watching closely.

A quiet irony sits at the center of the drama. Eli, Israel's high priest, sitting by the doorpost of the LORD's own house, cannot tell the difference between drunkenness and the deepest prayer he has ever witnessed, watching her mouth, verse 12, without understanding her heart, until Hannah must explain herself to the very man charged with discerning true worship. The narrator lets this misjudgment stand without excusing it, quietly preparing the reader for a priesthood, embodied fully in Eli's own sons two chapters later, that has grown unable to recognize real devotion when it is standing in front of them.
context.historical:
Elkanah's two wives reflect a hard reality Israel's law already anticipated: Deuteronomy 21:15-17 legislates for exactly this situation, a man with one loved and one unloved wife, assuming that polygamy driven by a first wife's barrenness was common enough to need regulating rather than an exotic exception. Peninnah's taunts fit a broader ancient pattern in which a second wife, brought in to secure an heir, could become a genuine rival once children arrived, since a wife's standing in the household often rose and fell with her ability to bear sons.

Hannah's manner of praying is itself a notable departure from expectation. Ancient prayer and vow making were normally spoken aloud, often with some public form; Eli's confusion in verses 13 and 14 makes sense precisely because a worshiper praying silently, lips moving without any sound, was unusual enough at Shiloh's sanctuary that the priest had no other category ready for it besides drunkenness. Hannah's silence becomes, unintentionally, a witness to how entirely private and unmediated her anguish before God had become.

Genealogically, 1 Chronicles 6:33-38 identifies this same family line as Levite, descended from Kohath, even though 1 Samuel 1:1 calls Elkanah an Ephraimite; Levites were assigned towns scattered among the other tribes rather than a single tribal territory, so a Levite family could be described by the region it lived in, Ephraim's hill country, without contradicting its priestly ancestry. That detail matters for Samuel's later ministry, since a boy from a Levite household serving at the sanctuary fits Israel's law far more naturally than an ordinary Ephraimite child would.

Finally, nursing in the ancient Near East typically continued for two to three years before a child was weaned, so the years between Hannah's vow and Samuel's arrival at Shiloh in verse 24 represent real, extended time in which she kept a promise long before she had to deliver on it publicly.
context.canonical:
Hannah's story deliberately joins a recognizable canonical succession of barren women whose sons became hinge figures in salvation history: Sarah and Isaac, Genesis 18:9-15 and 21:1-3, Rebekah and Jacob, Genesis 25:21, Rachel and Joseph, Genesis 30:22-24, and later Elizabeth and John the Baptist, Luke 1:5-25. Each time Scripture opens a new stage of its story with exactly this pattern, a womb the LORD alone can open, the reader is being taught in advance not to credit the coming deliverer to ordinary human planning; every one of these figures owes his existence, quite literally, to God's direct intervention rather than to nature running its expected course.

The chapter also looks forward within its own book. The prophet born here will anoint both of Israel's first two kings, Saul in 1 Samuel 10:1 and David in 1 Samuel 16:13, so that the boy whose birth answers one woman's prayer becomes, within a single generation, the instrument through which the entire monarchy is established. Hannah's private anguish at Shiloh and Israel's public transition from judges to kings turn out to be one connected story rather than two.

Canonically, the chapter also stands at Israel's own turning point between eras, closing the period the book of Judges describes as everyone doing right in his own eyes and opening the period of the monarchy that 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings will trace to its eventual end in exile. That this whole national hinge turns on the prayer of one overlooked woman, rather than on any recorded action of judge, priest, or army, sets the pattern the rest of the two books will keep testing: does Israel's future rest on the powerful, or on the LORD who hears the powerless.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Before the narrator ever records Samuel speaking a word, he wants his audience to already trust the boy's authority completely, and he builds that trust by placing Samuel's origin outside ordinary human decision from the very start. Every future scene in which Samuel rebukes Saul or anoints David draws its weight from this chapter, where the reader has already watched the LORD, not Elkanah's affection or Hannah's scheming, secure this child's existence. A hearer who has just watched Israel through Judges' downward spiral is meant to ask where a trustworthy voice could possibly come from in a nation like this, and the author answers, quietly, months before Samuel can speak: from a woman the official religious system had already failed to understand. The scene at Shiloh, where the reigning high priest cannot recognize true prayer without correction, is also intentional preparation; the very next chapter will expose Eli's own sons as worthless men who treat the LORD's offerings with contempt, and the author wants his audience to have already met, at Shiloh's threshold, one specimen of the priesthood's blindness before it is named outright.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Elkanah's two wives are described exactly as they were, with all the friction such a household produced, and the narrative's sympathy plainly lies with devoted love rather than with the arrangement itself; nothing here recommends polygamy as a pattern, any more than the taunting it produced is commended. Likewise, Hannah's specific vow, a lifelong Nazirite dedication for one particular son, was her own calling and not a template every praying parent must copy; not every answered prayer for a child obligates the parents to send that child away to lifelong sanctuary service. What does transfer to every reader is the shape of Hannah's response to unbearable provocation, taking her grief to the LORD rather than to bitterness or retaliation against Peninnah, and her willingness, once the prayer was answered, to actually keep the costly promise she had made rather than quietly renegotiating it once the ache had passed.

debates.question: Was Hannah's vow an attempt to bargain with God, or an act of surrendered faith?

views.label: A costly act of faith and surrender
views.case: Hannah asks for a son not to possess him but to give him back to the LORD for life; the vow's very shape, the longed-for gift returned to God, marks it as worship and surrender rather than a bargain struck for her own benefit.

views.label: A vow within ordinary Israelite piety
views.case: Vows were a recognized and permitted part of Old Testament worship, Numbers 30; Hannah is not manipulating God but bringing a heartfelt petition in the accepted form of her day, and God honors the faith beneath it.

debates.bearing: Either way the emphasis falls on God, who hears and gives, and on Hannah's readiness to give her dearest treasure back to Him; her prayer models honest, surrendered petition, not a transaction that obligates God.

debates.question: Why does the narrator dwell on Hannah rather than on the leaders of Israel?

views.label: To announce the book's theme of reversal
views.case: By opening with a barren, taunted woman rather than priest or judge, the narrator signals that God will raise up the lowly and bypass the proud, the very theme Hannah will sing in chapter 2 and that governs the whole book.

views.label: To contrast true faith with a failing sanctuary
views.case: Eli and his sons represent a priesthood in decline; Hannah's earnest, humble prayer shines against that failure, showing where real faith is found while official religion falters.

debates.bearing: Both readings prepare us to see that God's saving work advances through unexpected, humble people, and to look for the King He will raise up, ultimately Christ, born of a lowly woman.

study.originalLanguages:
Hannah's own name most likely comes from the root chanan, to show favor or grace, so that a woman named Grace opens the book by receiving none, at least from her rival, before the LORD gives her exactly what her name promised. The narrator never states the etymology outright, but a Hebrew ear would have heard the irony from the first verse: this Hannah's story is, in the end, about undeserved favor finally landing where it was named to land.

Her distress in verse 10 is described as bitter of nephesh, soul or whole life, wept before the LORD, and again in verse 15 as a woman troubled in ruach, spirit, praying out of the depth of her anguish. Nephesh names the whole self rather than a mere feeling, the same word used of the life breathed into Adam, Genesis 2:7, so that Hannah's grief is presented as reaching the entire core of who she is, not a passing sorrow she could simply set aside.

Verse 11 has her ask the LORD to look upon the oni, affliction, of His maidservant, the identical word Scripture uses of Israel's affliction in Egypt, Exodus 3:7, a word ordinarily reserved for genuinely severe, structural suffering rather than mild disappointment. By choosing it, Hannah places her private grief inside the same category of suffering the LORD is famous for answering on the nation's behalf.

The scene's turning hinge is a careful contrast between lev, heart, and qol, voice: Hannah was speaking in her lev, her lips moving, but her qol could not be heard, verse 13. Ancient prayer was ordinarily audible, so a heart that speaks without a voice describes something genuinely new in Israel's worship, prayer stripped down to its rawest form, communion with God that needs no witnesses and no words spoken aloud to be real and complete.

The chapter's four other key words each deserve their own weight. Tsebaoth, hosts, names the LORD as commander of every army in heaven and on earth, a title used here for the very first time in the whole Bible, striking given that it first appears attached to one grieving woman's prayer rather than to any battle. Nazir marks Samuel as belonging to the LORD in the same unbroken, lifelong way Samson had before him, Judges 13:5, though Samuel, unlike Samson, will keep the vow's spirit as faithfully as its outward sign. Zakar, remembered, always describes God moving to act rather than recalling something forgotten, exactly as it does when God remembered Noah, Genesis 8:1, and Israel in Egypt, Exodus 2:24. And shaal, to ask, threads the whole chapter together, naming both Samuel's origin, a son asked for, and his purpose, a son lent back, and will resurface soon in the very name of the king Israel itself will ask for, Saul, 1 Samuel 8:10 and following.

typology.type: The barren womb opened to give a deliverer
typology.fulfillment: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and now Hannah each receive a son central to Israel's future only after the LORD alone opens a womb nature had closed, a pattern too consistent across Scripture to be accidental. Luke deliberately places the announcement of Jesus' own birth to a virgin, an even more complete human impossibility than mere barrenness, in the same family of stories, Luke 1:34-35. The type reaches its limit and its escalation together: every earlier deliverer still required a human father, while the final Deliverer required none at all, so that His arrival owes even less to nature than Samuel's did.

Hannah's private anguish becomes, once answered, a public song celebrating a God who brings down the mighty and lifts the poor from the dust, 1 Samuel 2:4-8. Mary's Magnificat takes up the same movements almost verse for verse, scattering the proud, exalting the humble, filling the hungry, Luke 1:51-53, showing that Mary consciously prayed in Hannah's own voice at the announcement of a still greater reversal. The escalation is one of scope: Hannah's song answers one family's shame, Mary's answers the shame of the whole human race.

typology.type: Samuel dedicated wholly to the LORD before he could choose it himself
typology.fulfillment: Hannah gives Samuel to the LORD's service before he is old enough to consent, and he grows up doing exactly what was dedicated of him, ministering before the LORD, 1 Samuel 2:18, and later refusing to withhold a hard word even from the man who raised him, 1 Samuel 3:18. Christ's dedication to the Father's will was never imposed against His own choice, since He is Himself the eternal Son, yet He too was set apart from before His birth, Luke 1:32-33, and, unlike Samuel, never once wavered from doing exactly what He was given to do.

study.christ:
This chapter's failing sanctuary matters as much to its portrait of Christ as Hannah's prayer does. Eli, sitting at the doorpost of the LORD's house, cannot rightly discern a worshiper's heart, and his own sons will soon be shown treating the LORD's offerings with open contempt, 1 Samuel 2:12-17. Israel needed, and did not yet have, a priest who could perfectly recognize true devotion and never misuse what was entrusted to him. Hebrews later describes exactly such a priest in Jesus, one who sympathizes fully with human weakness, was tempted in every way yet without sin, and always lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him, Hebrews 4:15 and 7:25, everything Eli's house at Shiloh conspicuously was not.

Hannah's answered prayer also anticipates Christ by way of quiet preparation rather than direct announcement. No one at Shiloh that day, not Eli, not Elkanah, not even Hannah herself, has any idea that the child she is asking for will one day anoint the king from whose line the Messiah will come. The LORD is working a full generation ahead of anyone's awareness of it, exactly as He will later work through an unnoticed pregnancy in Nazareth and a quiet birth in Bethlehem, events that looked, at the time, like private family news rather than the hinge of the whole world's redemption.

There is a real correspondence, and a real difference, in the shape of dedication itself. Hannah gives back to the LORD the son she asked for, and Samuel spends his life doing exactly what was asked of him. The Son of God was never asked for by anyone; He was given, John 3:16, and He gives Himself back to the Father not because a parent's vow bound Him before He could object, but because eternal, willing obedience is simply who He is, I have come to do Your will, O God, Hebrews 10:7. Samuel's whole life traces, faintly and from a distance, the shape of a Son who is asked of no one, given by the Father's own initiative, and returned to Him in perfect, undivided obedience all the way to a cross.
study.god:
God's timing in this chapter is patient in a way that costs Hannah real years of grief; the narrator says this went on year after year, verse 7, before any resolution arrives, refusing to compress or excuse the length of her suffering. Scripture does not present God's compassion as something that always arrives on the timetable a sufferer would choose; Hannah waits, provoked and weeping, through repeated pilgrimages before the chapter's turning point, and the text never suggests her earlier years of prayer were wasted or unheard simply because the answer was delayed.

God's willingness to work through flawed instruments shows itself in Eli's blessing. Moments after misjudging Hannah as drunk, the very same priest, once corrected, speaks over her, go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him, verse 17, a word that turns out to be entirely true despite coming from a man who has just shown he cannot always tell true devotion from its counterfeit. God does not need a flawless mouthpiece to deliver a genuine blessing; He can speak truly even through someone whose own house, as the following chapters reveal, is already under coming judgment.

It is worth noticing where in Scripture the title LORD of Hosts first appears. Given a full introduction elsewhere to God's rule over the armies of heaven and earth, an Israelite might expect that title to debut on a battlefield. Instead it debuts in a private sanctuary courtyard, spoken by one weeping, childless woman making a vow no one else can hear, as though the narrator wants his first readers to learn, before any war story in this military age is told, that the commander of every army in existence is equally, fully present to a single person's smallest, most private sorrow.

That same God also keeps what is given back to Him rather than simply receiving it. Hannah releases Samuel into a corrupt sanctuary she has every reason to distrust, yet the boy is neither lost nor spoiled by that environment, because the LORD who granted the prayer also guards the child once he is handed over, a small but real assurance that what is entrusted to God in faith remains safe in His hands even when the surrounding institutions cannot be trusted at all.

crossReferences.note: Mary's Magnificat borrows the very shape of Hannah's prayer, my heart rejoices in the LORD, my horn is exalted, 1 Samuel 2:1, echoed in my soul magnifies the Lord. Both songs move from personal rescue to a sweeping reversal of the proud and the humble, showing Mary consciously praying in the cadence of a woman who prayed centuries before her.

God remembered Rachel and opened her womb, using the identical word for remembering used of Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:19. In both cases the LORD's remembering is not the end of forgetfulness but the beginning of decisive action, turning a season of barrenness into the birth of a son central to Israel's future.

The psalm celebrates a God who raises the poor from the dust and settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother. Hannah's own story supplies a living illustration of exactly this praise, a woman lifted from years of provocation and grief into the joy the psalmist describes in general terms.

Peter quotes the ancient proverb that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, promising that He exalts the humbled in due time. Hannah's years of humiliation before Peninnah, followed by exaltation as the mother of Israel's prophet, trace this exact pattern generations before Peter names it as a settled principle.

The law anticipates a household with one loved and one unloved wife and legislates fairly for the unloved wife's firstborn son, showing that the tension in Elkanah's home was common enough for Israel's law to address directly rather than a shocking exception invented for this story.

God remembered Noah and every living thing with him in the ark, causing the floodwaters to recede. The same verb used of Hannah describes God's decisive turn toward covenant faithfulness after a long, silent wait, showing that divine remembering consistently marks the hinge between hardship and a fresh act of deliverance.

An angel announces to Manoah's barren wife that her son will be a Nazirite from the womb who begins Israel's deliverance from the Philistines. Hannah's vow places Samuel under an identical lifelong consecration, and Scripture pointedly hands Israel back to back deliverers born through the same unmistakable pattern of barrenness answered by dedication.

Eli's own sons are introduced immediately after this chapter as wicked men who treat the LORD's offerings with contempt. Samuel's dedicated, faithful upbringing stands in deliberate, close contrast to the corrupt priesthood he is about to grow up alongside, sharpening the question of which kind of servant Israel actually needs.

The writer describes a high priest who sympathizes fully with human weakness and invites approach to God's throne with confidence. Eli's failure to recognize genuine anguish without correction, and his sons' abuse of the very sanctuary they served, throw into relief how much Israel needed exactly the priest Hebrews describes.

study.oneStory:
This chapter opens 1 and 2 Samuel by rewinding, in miniature, the whole shape of the biblical story: barrenness echoing the futility sin brought into a fruitful creation, Genesis 3:16-19, a cry brought honestly before God rather than resolved by human scheming, and a birth that becomes the hinge on which a much larger deliverance turns. Israel at this point looks very much like a fallen world in miniature, its judges spent, its priesthood compromised, its only king the LORD Himself, largely unacknowledged even at His own sanctuary.

The rescue that follows does not repair Israel by force or by a new law but by raising up, through answered prayer, one faithful voice inside a corrupt religious system, a pattern Scripture will repeat at each low point in its history, a remnant, a prophet, a child, appearing exactly when the visible institutions have failed to produce one. Samuel will anoint Saul and then David, and the line that begins with David's throne will run, through centuries of further failure, all the way to great David's greater Son.

The chapter's small domestic drama therefore turns out to sit precisely on redemption's timeline, after the fall's futility and before the covenant king's arrival, doing for Israel's monarchy what a similar prayer, centuries later, will do for the whole world: an unnoticed woman's plea becomes the occasion for God to move history forward by means no census or army would ever record.

And Hannah's example itself becomes part of the new creation's shape. The son she asks for and gives back anticipates every believer's proper posture toward whatever God gives, received with open, thankful hands and held loosely enough to be offered back to Him, until the day promised in Revelation when every tear Hannah or any other grieving mother ever shed is wiped away for good, Revelation 21:4, and nothing given to God is ever truly lost.

quiz.q: Why does the narrator open the book of 1 Samuel with Hannah rather than with a priest or judge?

options.text: To announce the book's theme that God lifts up the lowly and works His rescue through the humble and overlooked.
options.note: Hannah embodies the reversal she will sing in chapter 2, the key to the whole book.

options.text: To show that the priesthood at Shiloh was failing while true faith was found elsewhere.
options.note: True and part of the contrast, but the deeper point is the theme of God exalting the lowly.

options.text: Because Hannah was the most powerful person in Israel at the time.
options.note: The opposite is true; she was lowly and despised, which is precisely the point.

options.text: Because the birth of Samuel has nothing to do with the rest of the book.
options.note: Samuel is central; he will anoint Israel's first kings.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the LORD remembered Hannah?

options.text: God moved to act in covenant faithfulness on her behalf, giving her the son she asked for.
options.note: In Scripture God's remembering is the prelude to His saving action, as with Noah and Israel.

options.text: God gave her a son after she had prayed and vowed at Shiloh.
options.note: True in outcome, but understates that remembering means God acting in covenant care, not simply responding to the vow.

options.text: God had briefly forgotten Hannah and then recalled her situation.
options.note: God had not forgotten; remembering here is covenant action, not the ending of forgetfulness.

options.text: God rewarded Hannah because her bargain obligated Him to act.
options.note: The gift is God's gracious act, not a debt owed to a successful bargain.

quiz.q: What is the significance of Hannah's vow that no razor would touch her son's head?

options.text: She was setting Samuel apart to the LORD as a Nazirite, wholly consecrated to God for life.
options.note: The unshaven head marks the Nazirite vow, Numbers 6; Samuel belongs entirely to God.

options.text: She was promising to give her son to serve at the house of the LORD.
options.note: True in effect, but the specific sign named is the lifelong Nazirite consecration.

options.text: She was following a custom that had nothing to do with dedication to God.
options.note: It was precisely a sign of dedication, not an empty custom.

options.text: She was ensuring her son would become a wealthy and powerful man.
options.note: The vow gives him to God's service, not to worldly power.

quiz.q: How does Hannah's prayer and her son point forward in the story of salvation?

options.text: God giving a son to a lowly woman, and her song of reversal, anticipate Mary and the birth of Christ.
options.note: Hannah's song is echoed in Mary's Magnificat; God still lifts the lowly and gives the promised Son.

options.text: They show that God sometimes answers the prayers of those who are sad.
options.note: True but thin; the passage points to God's larger pattern of salvation through the humble.

options.text: They teach that anyone who makes a vow will receive whatever they ask.
options.note: This misreads the vow as a formula; the emphasis is on God's gracious giving.

options.text: They have no connection to the coming of Christ.
options.note: The birth of a deliverer to a lowly woman clearly foreshadows the gospel.

quiz.q: What does this chapter reveal about God?

options.text: He is the LORD of Hosts, sovereign over all, yet He bends low to hear one forgotten, weeping woman.
options.note: The chapter holds together God's majesty and His tender nearness to the lowly.

options.text: He is a God who opens and closes the womb, so that life is His gift.
options.note: True and important, but only part of the fuller picture of His majesty joined to His nearness.

options.text: He is a distant ruler who only concerns Himself with kings and armies.
options.note: The chapter shows the opposite; the LORD of Hosts hears one grieving woman.

options.text: He is unable to help the barren or the brokenhearted.
options.note: He is precisely the One who gives life and lifts the lowly.

questions: Hannah brought her deepest grief straight to the LORD and poured out her soul before Him. Where do you need to stop carrying your sorrow alone and bring it honestly to God?
Peninnah's taunts drove Hannah to prayer rather than away from God. How can the very things that provoke and wound you become the occasion to seek the LORD more earnestly?
Hannah asked for a son and then gave him back to God. What is the treasure you are most tempted to grasp, and what would it look like to hold it before God with open hands?
The LORD remembered Hannah and acted. How does it steady you to know that God's remembering His people is always the beginning of His saving work, even when the answer is slow?
God began Israel's rescue through a lowly, overlooked woman. Where are you tempted to think God only works through the impressive and powerful, and how does this chapter correct that?

translationNotes.note: Ramathaim-zophim is a place name; the BSB footnote notes it may read from Ramathaim, a Zuphite, comparing the Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 6.
A double portion follows the BSB reading; the footnote allows a choice portion, marking Elkanah's special love for Hannah either way.
The name Samuel sounds like the Hebrew for heard of God; Hannah links it to her asking, since the same root, shaal, means to ask and to lend or dedicate.
Some Dead Sea Scrolls add that Hannah would offer him as a Nazirite for all time, making explicit the lifelong consecration implied in her vow of verse 11.
